sweep_summary: Hausa (haus1257) is in the catalog as 'tonal', deciding source Caron 2015 (a tone description). Of 23 title-hits, 4 were read in full: Hunter 1980 (already held by the project and already listed) is the key first-hand stress source and CONFIRMS the classification — an instrumental refutation of Abraham's stress claims, concluding 'there is no need for both tone and stress to describe Hausa' (p. 372); Leben 1996 (newly downloaded, SAL open access) CONFIRMS with 'Hausa has High and Low lexical tones but no phonological stress' (p. 139); Alidou 1995 (KU, image-only, scanned) and Churma 1975 (OSU KB) are prosodic-morphology and tone-representation papers, silent on stress. Schuh 1989's Glottolog title 'verb prosody' is a typo for 'verse prosody: Mutadaarik' (Crossref, same pages), so it, Greenberg 1949 and Schuh 1999 are verse-metre noise. Not obtainable: Leben 1980 LI (JSTOR) and Möhlig 1983 (Buske print) are the only two worth acquiring (medium); Inkelas 1988, Bature 1990, Levin 1979/80, Leben 2003 low; the rest (Ayers 1996 English dissertation, Davis 2008 OHG, Ellis 2009 semantic prosody, Baker & Smith 1976 English) are misattached and irrelevant. Recommendation: keep 'tonal'; promote Hunter 1980 p. 372 (with Leben 1996 p. 139) to the deciding stress quotation. lookups used Crossref/Glottolog/DSpace APIs and direct downloads.

sources.quote: The results of the experiment on stress in Hausa lead to the conclusions that while there are contextually conditioned pronunciation changes which occur in certain grammatical constructions in Hausa, these changes cannot appropriately be described in terms of stress but rather must be considered tonal changes. There is no need therefore for both tone and stress to describe Hausa. Furthermore, the "prominence" which occurs behaves linguistically like tone and not like stress.
sources.locator: abstract p. 353; sec. 4 General Conclusions p. 372
sources.note: Instrumental (F0 + duration) test of Abraham's 1934/1959 claim that High-toned syllables are stressed and that stress shifts in LH nouns/verbs before an initial-H word. Pitch of LH and HL words is affected by the following word's initial tone, but duration is not; the effects are general tone/pitch-realization rules. Conclusion: no stress feature is needed for Hausa; the earlier 'stress' reports (Taylor 1923, Abraham, Pilszczikowa 1968, Wangler 1963, Kraft & Kraft 1973) are reviewed on pp. 353-355 as tone-correlated prominence.

tone.quote: Ne,'IDan and Newman [1981] mention three distinct prosodic gestures that can be involved in Hausa questions: a 10w tone, added to the rightmost High tone in the utterance; length, added to the final syllable of the utterance if it is not already long; and key raising, an upward shift in the pitch levels of Hand 1. Note that these three gestures are quite distinct. For one thing, length is added to the final syllable, while the Low tone is added to the final high-toned syllable. … Thus, phrase tones and boundary tones both appear to function in Hausa intonation.

tone.quote: The aspects of the language discussed are the phonology and morphology. While syntax is not taken up in any detail, tone is not even discussed. In the case of tone the reason is that tonal differences do not enter into dialectal differences either generally or in any systematic way. Furthermore there is as yet no agreed way within generative phonology for the treatment of tone. And indeed it is too vast a subject for one thesis to handle adequately.
